sources.title: Oribi
sources.note: Cites the 2016 IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group assessment of Least Concern, with a 2008 global estimate of about 750,000 animals.

size.note: Shoulder height is given as 50–67 cm in one compilation and 50–66 cm in another; both are recorded and are not averaged, and the wider published range is stored. Head-and-body length 92–110 cm and mass 12–22 kg are given in both accounts. Male horn length is given as 8–18 cm in one compilation (with a recorded maximum of 19.1 cm from Malawi) and 8–19 cm in another. No tail length was found. Males are described as slightly smaller than females, except in O. o. ourebi, in which females are smaller.

summary: A small, slender antelope with a glossy yellowish to rufous-brown coat, white underparts and rump, a short dark tail and a white stripe over each eye. Only males have thin, straight horns. It lives in open grassland with a mix of short and tall grass, and is listed as Endangered in the region.
description: A small, long-legged antelope with a slightly raised back and a long neck. The glossy coat is yellowish to rufous brown; the southern subspecies O. o. ourebi is described as a rich rufous. The chin, throat, underparts and rump are white, and a white line of fur runs over each eye. A bare dark patch lies beneath each ear, and there is a tuft of long hair on each knee. The bushy tail is brown to black on the outside with a white underside in most subspecies (one compilation simply calls it a short black tail). Only males have horns: thin and straight, ringed at the base and smooth at the tips, with published lengths of 8–18 cm or 8–19 cm. Prominent preorbital glands appear as vertical folds on the side of the face. Females have four teats and no horns.
habits: Active mainly by day, with some activity also observed at night, and it rests in cover during rain. It lives alone, in pairs, or in small groups; one account gives herds of up to four, another up to six. Males defend a territory of 25–100 ha and mark vegetation and soil with preorbital-gland secretions, urine and dung; all animals may gather at temporary dung middens. Unlike other small antelopes, oribi may be polyandrous, polygynous or polygynandrous, depending on the habitat. Recently burnt grassland often attracts groups. Sources disagree on some social details, and both accounts are kept.

diet.summary: Primarily a grazer that prefers fresh grasses, which can make up as much as 90% of the diet, and browses more when fresh grass is scarce. Preferred grasses include Andropogon, Eulalia, Hyparrhenia, Loudetia, Pennisetum and Themeda. It also visits mineral licks, and has been seen feeding on flowers and Boletus mushrooms.
items: fresh grasses (Andropogon, Eulalia, Hyparrhenia, Loudetia, Pennisetum, Themeda)

young: A single calf is born after a gestation of six to seven months. In southern Africa, births are described as peaking from November to December in one compilation; another gives a breeding peak in October and November and says mating can occur year-round. Mating may also peak in the rainy season (August to September). The newborn is kept in concealment for nearly a month, and the mother returns to suckle it. Weaning is at four to five months. One account says both sexes mature at 10–14 months; another gives about 10 months for females and 14 months for males. Those disagreements are recorded and are not averaged. A Kruger-specific birth-month range was not found. Skinner and Chimimba (2005, p. 698) record mating in April–June in the KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg and in May in Mpumalanga, so most lambs arrive in the warm, wet months from October to December; they give a gestation of about 210 days and a single young that the female hides in grass.

habitat: Open grassland, floodplains and savanna woodland with a mosaic of short grass for feeding and taller grass for cover, including recently burnt ground; steep slopes are avoided. In South Africa it occurs mainly in grasslands of Mpumalanga, the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, and also in the southern and northeastern Free State and southern Limpopo. A Kruger-specific habitat account was not found.

similar.note: The oribi is larger, with a longer neck, a short dark tail that is white underneath in most accounts, a bare dark patch below each ear, a white stripe over the eye, and a tuft of hair on each knee. Only male oribi have thin, straight horns.
Sharpe's grysbok is a smaller antelope. The oribi has a glossy yellowish to rufous coat with clear white underparts and rump, a short dark tail, and a white stripe over the eye.
Grey rhebok is a greyer antelope. The oribi is yellowish to rufous brown with white underparts and rump and a short dark tail.

population.notes: No Kruger population figure was found. The species is on the official 2011 checklist. One source claims a number of oribi were moved from the Badplaas area to an enclosure at Pretoriuskop, with limited success. The 2025 regional assessment does not mention Kruger; it gives a regional minimum of 3,098 individuals in 2013–2015 (1,859–2,169 mature individuals) and a declining regional trend. Those regional totals, and a global estimate of about 750,000 animals from 2008, are not a park census. Regional Red List status is Endangered. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf

viewNotes.note: A slender build with a long neck and long legs, a slightly raised back, a yellowish to rufous coat, white underparts and rump, and a short dark tail. A white stripe sits over each eye, and a bare dark patch lies below each ear.
Thin, straight horns, a white stripe over each eye, and prominent preorbital glands on the side of the face.

calls.description: Animals at least three months old may give one to three alarm whistles on sensing danger. The whistles are more common in adults than in juveniles, and males appear to whistle more.

One source claims a translocation from Badplaas to an enclosure at Pretoriuskop, with limited success. Status and monthsPresent are omitted rather than guessed. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. The 2016 assessment does not mention Kruger National Park. The 2011 checklist is the only Kruger listing and was not used. A tourism-page translocation claim remains unused. Status and monthsPresent remain omitted.

Sources disagree on shoulder height (50–67 cm versus 50–66 cm), male horn length (8–18 cm versus 8–19 cm), tail colour (brown to black with a white underside versus a short black tail), group size (up to four versus up to six), and breeding peak (births November–December in southern Africa versus a peak in October–November, with maturity at 10–14 months versus 10 months in females and 14 months for males); both accounts are recorded and are not averaged.
No tail length or sexed shoulder-height or mass split was found, so those fields are omitted or stored only as unsexed ranges.

iNaturalist has 0 sound observations for Ourebia ourebi in place 69020. No reusable Kruger recording was found. Call types are limited to the alarm whistle described in compiled accounts.
